claims.claim: Isaiah 56–66 is dated by most scholars to c. 530–500 BC; chs 40–55 to an exilic prophet.
claims.source: Standard introductions, e.g. J. Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 56–66 (Anchor, 2003); traditional single-author view noted.

claims.claim: Ezekiel was taken to Babylon with the exiles of 597 BC.
claims.source: Ezekiel 1:1–3; 2 Kings 24:10–16.

claims.claim: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC; second Temple completed 515 BC.
claims.source: Cyrus Cylinder; Ezra 6:15; standard histories.

claims.claim: Daniel's visions reached their final form under Antiochus IV, 167–164 BC (majority view).
claims.source: J. J. Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia, 1993).

claims.claim: 2 Maccabees 7: the second son says the King of the universe will raise those who die for his laws.
claims.source: 2 Maccabees 7:9.

claims.claim: Pharisees affirmed and Sadducees denied the resurrection.
claims.source: Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8; Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.3–4.

claims.claim: The thirteenth of Maimonides' principles (1168) is the resurrection of the dead.
claims.source: Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10 (Perek Helek).

claims.claim: The Amidah's second blessing praises God who gives life to the dead; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 denies a share in the world to come to those who deny the resurrection.
claims.source: Siddur, Amidah, Gevurot; m. Sanhedrin 10:1.

claims.claim: Hesiod's myth of the ages; Virgil's Fourth Eclogue (c. 40 BC) read by medieval Christians as messianic.
claims.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 109–201; Virgil, Eclogue 4; Augustine, City of God X.27.

claims.claim: Possible Zoroastrian influence on resurrection belief is debated.
claims.source: M. Boyce, Zoroastrians (1979); J. D. Levenson, Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel (2006).

claims.claim: Edward Hicks painted more than sixty versions of the Peaceable Kingdom; the background group is Penn's treaty with the Lenape.
claims.source: National Gallery of Art collection notes on Hicks; the NGA description says only 'indigenous people' and 'men in tricorn hats'.

claims.claim: Collins's 1979 definition of the apocalypse genre.
claims.source: J. J. Collins (ed.), Semeia 14 (1979).

claims.claim: Justin and Irenaeus identify the author of Revelation with the apostle; Dionysius of Alexandria argued for another John on grounds of style.
claims.source: Justin, Dialogue 81; Irenaeus, Against Heresies IV.20.11; Eusebius, Church History VII.25.

claims.claim: Irenaeus dates the vision to the end of Domitian's reign and knows the variant 616.
claims.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.30.1, V.30.3.

claims.claim: 666 = 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr); 616 corresponds to the Latin spelling.
claims.source: R. Bauckham, The Climax of Prophecy (1993), ch. 11; Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 4499 reads 616.

claims.claim: Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of Rome, AD 64.
claims.source: Tacitus, Annals XV.44.

claims.claim: Tertullian says John was banished to an island after surviving an attempt on his life in Rome.
claims.source: Tertullian, The Prescription against Heretics 36.

claims.claim: Patmos: Cave of the Apocalypse and Monastery of St John (founded 1088); UNESCO World Heritage Site.
claims.source: UNESCO listing 942 (1999).

claims.claim: 1 Enoch 1:9 is quoted in Jude 14–15; Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch at Qumran (at least eleven manuscripts); complete only in Ge'ez; canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches.
claims.source: G. W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001), introduction; J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch (1976).

claims.claim: Book of the Watchers dated to the 200s BC.
claims.source: Nickelsburg (2001).

claims.claim: Tertullian argued for accepting Enoch partly because Jude quotes it.
claims.source: Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women I.3.

claims.claim: Eusebius lists Revelation among accepted and, 'if it seem proper', disputed books; Cyril of Jerusalem omits it; it is not read in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History III.25; Cyril, Catechetical Lectures 4.36.

claims.claim: Luther's 1522 preface doubted Revelation; his 1530 preface read it as Church history; Calvin wrote no commentary on it.
claims.source: Luther's Works 35:398–411; T. H. L. Parker, Calvin's New Testament Commentaries.

claims.claim: Messiaen's Quartet for the End of Time, inspired by Revelation 10, was first performed in Stalag VIII-A on 15 January 1941.
claims.source: Rebecca Rischin, For the End of Time (2003).

claims.claim: Herod began rebuilding the Temple c. 20 BC; Western Wall stones are among the largest in the ancient world.
claims.source: Josephus, Antiquities 15.11; standard archaeological surveys.

claims.claim: Titus destroyed the Temple in August AD 70; the Arch of Titus (c. AD 81) shows the menorah carried off.
claims.source: Josephus, Jewish War VI.4–5; the Arch of Titus, Rome.

claims.claim: Eusebius reports the flight of the Jerusalem Christians to Pella.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History III.5.3.

claims.claim: Jesus son of Ananias foretold the Temple's fall in the 60s.
claims.source: Josephus, Jewish War VI.5.3.

claims.claim: Theudas (c. AD 45), 'the Egyptian' (c. AD 55), and a false prophet during the siege.
claims.source: Josephus, Antiquities 20.5.1, 20.8.6; Jewish War II.13.5, VI.5.2; Acts 5:36; 21:38.

claims.claim: Athanasius explained Mark 13:32 as ignorance in Christ's human nature.
claims.source: Athanasius, Against the Arians III.42–46.

claims.claim: William Miller predicted 1843, then 22 October 1844 (the Great Disappointment).
claims.source: D. L. Rowe, God's Strange Work (2008).

claims.claim: Abraham Davenport and the Dark Day of 19 May 1780.
claims.source: Timothy Dwight's account; J. G. Whittier, 'Abraham Davenport'.

claims.claim: Bach's Wachet auf (BWV 140), 1731, on Nicolai's hymn of 1599.
claims.source: Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis; standard Bach scholarship.

claims.claim: 1 Thessalonians c. AD 50 is probably the oldest surviving Christian writing; 2 Corinthians c. 55–56; Romans c. 57.
claims.source: Standard New Testament introductions, e.g. R. E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (1997).

claims.claim: The Latin epitaph formula 'non fui, fui, non sum, non curo'; 'cemetery' from Greek koimētērion.
claims.source: Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum (many examples); Oxford English Dictionary.

claims.claim: Apantēsis used of civic welcome of a dignitary.
claims.source: E. Peterson, Zeitschrift für systematische Theologie 7 (1930); F. F. Bruce, 1 and 2 Thessalonians (1982).

claims.claim: Rapture: from Latin rapiemur (Vulgate 1 Thess 4:17); developed by J. N. Darby in the 1830s; spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and the Left Behind novels (1995–2007).
claims.source: T. P. Weber, On the Road to Armageddon (2004); B. Rossing, The Rapture Exposed (2004).

claims.claim: Purgatory taught by Catholics (Florence 1439, Trent Session 25); Orthodox pray for the dead without defined purgatory; soul sleep among Seventh-day Adventists.
claims.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030–1032; T. Ware, The Orthodox Church; Adventist Fundamental Beliefs 26.

claims.claim: Irenaeus taught renewal, not annihilation, of creation; Aquinas likewise.
claims.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.32–36; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae Suppl. q. 91.

claims.claim: Augustine thought martyrs' wounds would be seen in glory.
claims.source: Augustine, City of God XXII.19.

claims.claim: 1662 BCP burial: 'in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life'.
claims.source: Book of Common Prayer (1662), Burial of the Dead.

claims.claim: Wright's phrase 'life after life after death'.
claims.source: N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) and Surprised by Hope (2008).

claims.claim: Oldest manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 read 'will be found'.
claims.source: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; B. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament.

claims.claim: Reimarus (1694–1768); Lessing published the fragments 1774–78; Weiss 1892.
claims.source: C. H. Talbert (ed.), Reimarus: Fragments (1970); J. Weiss, Die Predigt Jesu vom Reiche Gottes (1892).

claims.claim: Schweitzer (1875–1965): Von Reimarus zu Wrede (1906), tr. Montgomery 1910; Lambaréné 1913; Nobel Peace Prize for 1952 (awarded 1953).
claims.source: Gutenberg #45422 header; nobelprize.org.

claims.claim: Russell's lecture 'Why I Am Not a Christian', Battersea Town Hall, 6 March 1927; argued Jesus expected his second coming within his hearers' lifetimes, citing Matthew 10:23 and 16:28.
claims.source: Russell, Why I Am Not a Christian and Other Essays (1957). Our own words only (Russell d. 1970).

claims.claim: C. S. Lewis called Mark 13:30 'the most embarrassing verse in the Bible' (one short quotation, under 25 words).
claims.source: Lewis, 'The World's Last Night' (first published 1952 as 'Christian Hope: Its Meaning for Today', Religion in Life); in The World's Last Night and Other Essays (1960).

claims.claim: Dodd's realised eschatology (1935); Cullmann's D-Day/V-Day (Christ and Time, 1946).
claims.source: C. H. Dodd, The Parables of the Kingdom; O. Cullmann, Christ and Time.

claims.claim: Allison and Ehrman on Jesus as apocalyptic prophet.
claims.source: D. C. Allison, Jesus of Nazareth: Millenarian Prophet (1998); B. D. Ehrman, Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium (1999).

claims.claim: Chrysostom read Matthew 16:28 as fulfilled in the transfiguration.
claims.source: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 56.

claims.claim: Augustine: bishop of Hippo 395–430; City of God 413–426; once held the millennial view.
claims.source: Augustine, City of God XX.7; P. Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967).

claims.claim: Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian held an earthly millennium; Tyconius read Revelation of the Church.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History III.39; Justin, Dialogue 80–81; Irenaeus V.32–36; Tertullian, Against Marcion III.24; B. Daley, The Hope of the Early Church (1991).

claims.claim: Pergamum's temple to Rome and Augustus, 29 BC.
claims.source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 51.20; S. R. F. Price, Rituals and Power (1984).

claims.claim: All Saints: Gregory III's chapel in St Peter's (731–741) dedicated 1 November; feast spread in the Frankish empire c. 835; Orthodox keep it on the Sunday after Pentecost.
claims.source: Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, 'All Saints' Day'.

claims.claim: Westminster Shorter Catechism Q1 (1647).
claims.source: Westminster Shorter Catechism.

claims.claim: Catechism 676 rejects even modified millenarianism; Augsburg Confession XVII rejects an earthly kingdom of the godly before the resurrection.
claims.source: CCC 676; Augsburg Confession (1530), art. XVII.

claims.claim: Universalism from Origen; anathemas associated with Constantinople 553; Gregory of Nyssa's hope of restoration.
claims.source: Daley (1991); the fifteen anathemas against Origen (553).

claims.claim: Whitby (1703) and Jonathan Edwards as postmillennialists.
claims.source: D. Whitby, Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament (1703); Edwards, A History of the Work of Redemption.

claims.claim: Münster 1534–35; Waco 19 April 1993: seventy-six died, about twenty-five of them children.
claims.source: N. Cohn, The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957); US Department of Justice report on Waco (1993); Tabor and Gallagher, Why Waco? (1995).

claims.claim: Hopkins wrote 'The Wreck of the Deutschland' 1875–76; refused by The Month; first published 1918 by Bridges; the Deutschland ran aground on the Kentish Knock on 6 December 1875; five Franciscan nuns drowned; one reportedly cried 'O Christ, Christ, come quickly'.
claims.source: Gutenberg #22403 (Bridges's notes); The Times, 11 December 1875; N. H. MacKenzie, A Reader's Guide to G. M. Hopkins (1981).

claims.claim: Feuerbach (1841), Freud (1927), Nietzsche (Zarathustra, Prologue 3, 1883), Marx ('opium of the people', 1844); Moltmann (1964; d. 2024).
claims.source: The works as cited; our own words.

claims.claim: Käsemann: 'Apocalyptic is the mother of all Christian theology' (exam question).
claims.source: E. Käsemann, 'The Beginnings of Christian Theology' (1960), in New Testament Questions of Today (1969).

claims.claim: Music facts: Haydn's Creation 1798; Brahms's German Requiem 1868 with its texts; Mozart died 1791 with the Requiem unfinished; How's 'For all the saints' 1864 to Vaughan Williams's Sine Nomine 1906; Messiah 1741 ends with 'Worthy is the Lamb' and Amen.
claims.source: Standard reference works (Grove).
